title: In-Memory Database Caching Architecture Workshop
content:
In-Memory Database Caching Architecture Workshop Overview This hands-on workshop guides you through building a production-ready multi-layer caching architecture using Amazon ElastiCache, DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX), and CloudFront. You’ll gain practical experience optimizing application performance and reducing database load by up to 90%.
Performance Focus: This workshop demonstrates industry-standard caching patterns and AWS best practices for achieving sub-millisecond response times and handling high-traffic applications.
Workshop Modules Introduction and Architecture Overview Setup VPC and Network Infrastructure Setup DynamoDB and DAX Setup ElastiCache Redis Setup Application Server Setup Application Load Balancer Setup CloudFront CDN Performance Testing and Analysis Monitoring and Alerting Resource Cleanup and Best Practices Throughout this workshop, you’ll learn techniques for designing high-performance caching architectures that can be applied to your own production environments, achieving 90%+ cache hit ratios and 50%+ faster response times.
Workshop Duration: 3-4 hours | Cost: ~$1-2 USD

title: 1. Introduction
content:
Introduction Multi-Layer Caching Architecture What is Multi-Layer Caching? Multi-layer caching is a performance optimization strategy that uses multiple levels of cache storage to reduce latency and improve application responsiveness. Each layer serves different purposes and has different characteristics, working together to provide optimal performance.
Key Capabilities With multi-layer caching architecture, you can achieve:
Dramatic performance improvements with sub-millisecond response times Significant cost reduction by reducing database load by up to 70% Enhanced scalability to handle 10x more concurrent users High availability with automatic failover across multiple cache layers Intelligent cache management with automatic data population and invalidation Architecture Fundamentals Performance Focus: Each cache layer is strategically positioned to intercept requests at different points in the application stack, maximizing cache hit ratios and minimizing response times.
Our architecture consists of three distinct caching layers:
CloudFront (L0 Cache): Global edge caching with 10-50ms latency ElastiCache Redis (L1 Cache): Application-level caching with sub-millisecond latency DynamoDB DAX (L2 Cache): Database-level caching with microsecond latency Cache layers are designed to work together, with each layer having specific:
TTL (Time To Live) settings ranging from 5 minutes to 24 hours Capacity limits based on memory allocation and node types Eviction policies to manage memory efficiently Cache Consistency: Proper cache invalidation strategies are crucial to maintain data consistency across all layers while maximizing performance benefits.
Caching Evolution Modern applications require sophisticated caching strategies due to:
Increased user expectations for instant response times Growing data volumes that strain traditional database systems Global user bases requiring low-latency access worldwide Cost optimization needs to reduce infrastructure expenses Multi-layer caching addresses these challenges by implementing intelligent data placement and retrieval strategies.
Best Practice: While single-layer caching provides some benefits, multi-layer architectures can achieve 90%+ cache hit ratios and 50%+ performance improvements compared to non-cached systems.
Workshop Contents In the following sections, we will explore these fundamental caching components:
VPC and Network Infrastructure DynamoDB and DAX Configuration ElastiCache Redis Setup Application Integration CloudFront Distribution Performance Testing and Monitoring Introduction Modules Workshop Overview Architecture Overview

title: 1.2 Architecture Overview
content:
Complete Architecture Diagram Our multi-layer caching architecture consists of three main caching layers, each serving a specific purpose in the performance optimization strategy.
Layer 0: CloudFront (Global Edge Cache) Purpose CloudFront serves as the global content delivery network (CDN) that caches content at edge locations worldwide.
Characteristics Latency: 10-50ms (depending on edge location) TTL: 5 minutes to 24 hours Scope: Global distribution Best for: Static content, API responses, images Benefits Reduces origin server load Improves global performance Handles traffic spikes DDoS protection Layer 1: ElastiCache Redis (Application Cache) Purpose Redis provides fast, in-memory caching for frequently accessed application data.
Characteristics Latency: Sub-millisecond TTL: 5 minutes to 1 hour Scope: Regional Best for: Session data, computed results, hot data Benefits Extremely fast data access Supports complex data structures Built-in replication and failover Pub/sub messaging capabilities Layer 2: DynamoDB DAX (Database Cache) Purpose DAX provides microsecond-latency caching specifically for DynamoDB operations.
Characteristics Latency: Microseconds TTL: Automatic (write-through) Scope: Regional Best for: DynamoDB queries, hot partitions Benefits Seamless DynamoDB integration No application code changes required Automatic cache management Multi-AZ availability Cache Population Strategy Cache-Aside Pattern: Application manages cache population Write-Through: DAX automatically caches writes Lazy Loading: Populate cache on first miss Cache Warming: Pre-populate frequently accessed data Network Architecture VPC Design Public Subnets: Load Balancer, NAT Gateways Private Subnets: Application servers, ElastiCache, DAX Multi-AZ: High availability across availability zones Security Groups: Least-privilege network access Security Considerations Encryption: At rest and in transit Network Isolation: Private subnets for backend services IAM Roles: Service-specific permissions Security Groups: Port-specific access control Performance Characteristics Expected Performance Metrics Layer Latency Throughput Hit Ratio Target CloudFront 10-50ms 100K+ RPS 80%+ Redis <1ms 100K+ OPS 90%+ DAX <1ms 1M+ OPS 95%+ DynamoDB 1-10ms Variable N/A Cache Hit Ratio Optimization Target Overall Hit Ratio: 90%+ Redis Hit Ratio: 85%+ DAX Hit Ratio: 95%+ CloudFront Hit Ratio: 80%+ Monitoring and Observability Key Metrics to Monitor Cache Hit Ratios
CloudFront cache hit rate Redis cache hit/miss ratio DAX cache effectiveness Performance Metrics
Response times per layer Throughput per service Error rates and timeouts Cost Metrics
Data transfer costs Compute costs per layer Storage costs Alerting Strategy Low Cache Hit Rate: < 80% overall High Latency: > 100ms response time Error Rate: > 1% error rate Cost Anomalies: Unexpected cost increases Scalability Considerations Horizontal Scaling Application Tier: Auto Scaling Groups Cache Tier: Redis cluster mode Database Tier: DynamoDB auto-scaling Vertical Scaling Instance Types: Upgrade based on memory/CPU needs Cache Size: Increase memory allocation Network: Enhanced networking for high throughput Disaster Recovery Multi-AZ Deployment ElastiCache: Cross-AZ replication DAX: Multi-AZ cluster nodes DynamoDB: Global tables (optional) Application: Multi-AZ deployment Backup Strategy DynamoDB: Point-in-time recovery ElastiCache: Automated backups Application: AMI snapshots Configuration: Infrastructure as Code This architecture is designed for high availability, performance, and cost optimization. Each layer serves a specific purpose in the overall caching strategy.

title: 2. Setup VPC and Network Infrastructure
content:
Setup VPC and Network Infrastructure In this section, we’ll create the foundational network infrastructure for our multi-layer caching architecture. We’ll set up a secure, highly available VPC with proper subnet distribution across multiple Availability Zones.
Network Architecture Overview Our VPC infrastructure includes:
VPC: Isolated virtual network with CIDR 10.0.0.0/16 Multi-AZ Design: Resources distributed across 2 Availability Zones for high availability Public Subnets: For internet-facing resources like Load Balancer Private Subnets: For backend services like ElastiCache, DAX, and application servers Internet Gateway: Provides internet access for public resources NAT Gateways: Enable secure outbound internet access for private resources Security Groups Strategy We’ll create dedicated security groups for each service:
ALB Security Group: Allows HTTP/HTTPS traffic from internet Application Security Group: Allows traffic from ALB and internal services Redis Security Group: Allows Redis traffic (port 6379) from application DAX Security Group: Allows DAX traffic (port 8111) from application High Availability Design Our network provides:
Cross-AZ Redundancy: Resources span multiple Availability Zones Fault Tolerance: NAT Gateway in each AZ for redundancy Scalability: Subnets sized appropriately for future growth Security: Private subnets isolate backend services from direct internet access Network Benefits This architecture delivers:
Security: Multi-layer security with security groups and private subnets Performance: Low-latency communication between services in same VPC Reliability: Multi-AZ deployment eliminates single points of failure Cost Optimization: Efficient use of NAT Gateways and subnet allocation Setup Steps Create VPC - Set up the VPC with subnets, gateways, and routing Create Security Groups - Configure network security for all services This VPC design follows AWS Well-Architected Framework principles for security, reliability, and performance efficiency.

title: 2.1 Create VPC
content:
In this step, we’ll create a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) with all the necessary networking components for our multi-layer caching architecture.
Step 1: Navigate to VPC Console Open the AWS Management Console Navigate to the VPC service Click Create VPC Step 2: Choose VPC Creation Method Select VPC and more to create VPC with associated resources The “VPC and more” option automatically creates subnets, route tables, internet gateway, and NAT gateways, saving time and ensuring proper configuration.
Step 3: Configure VPC Settings Basic VPC Configuration Configure the basic VPC settings:
Name tag auto-generation: caching-workshop IPv4 CIDR block: 10.0.0.0/16 IPv6 CIDR block: No IPv6 CIDR block Tenancy: Default Subnet Configuration Configure subnets for high availability:
Number of Availability Zones: 2 Number of public subnets: 2 Number of private subnets: 2 NAT Gateway Configuration Configure NAT gateways for outbound internet access:
NAT gateways: 1 per AZ VPC endpoints: None (for this workshop) Using 1 NAT gateway per AZ provides high availability but increases costs. For cost optimization in non-production environments, you could use 1 NAT gateway total.
Step 4: Create VPC Click Create VPC VPC creation will take 2-3 minutes. The process creates all associated resources including subnets, route tables, internet gateway, and NAT gateways.
Step 5: Verify VPC Creation Once created, you’ll see the success message: Click View VPC to see the created resources Step 6: Explore Created Resources VPC Dashboard Navigate to the VPC Dashboard to see all created resources: Subnets Overview Check the Subnets section to verify proper distribution: Verify you have:
2 Public subnets in different AZs 2 Private subnets in different AZs Proper CIDR allocation (e.g., 10.0.1.0/24, 10.0.2.0/24, etc.) Route Tables Check Route Tables to ensure proper routing: Verify:
Public route table: Routes 0.0.0.0/0 to Internet Gateway Private route tables: Route 0.0.0.0/0 to NAT Gateways Internet Gateway Verify the Internet Gateway is attached: NAT Gateways Check NAT Gateways are created in public subnets: Step 7: Document Important Information Record the following information for use in subsequent steps:
VPC Information VPC ID: vpc-xxxxxxxxx VPC CIDR: 10.0.0.0/16 Subnet Information Public Subnet 1: subnet-xxxxxxxxx (AZ: us-east-1a) Public Subnet 2: subnet-xxxxxxxxx (AZ: us-east-1b) Private Subnet 1: subnet-xxxxxxxxx (AZ: us-east-1a) Private Subnet 2: subnet-xxxxxxxxx (AZ: us-east-1b) Keep this information handy as you’ll need these IDs when creating security groups, launching instances, and configuring other AWS services.
Troubleshooting Common Issues Issue: VPC Creation Fails Possible Causes:
Insufficient permissions CIDR block conflicts Service limits reached Solutions:
Verify IAM permissions include VPC creation rights Choose a different CIDR block Check AWS service limits in your account Issue: NAT Gateway Creation Fails Possible Causes:
Insufficient Elastic IP addresses Public subnet not properly configured Solutions:
Request additional Elastic IP addresses Verify public subnets have routes to Internet Gateway Next Steps Your VPC infrastructure is now ready! You have:
✅ VPC with proper CIDR allocation
✅ Multi-AZ deployment for high availability
✅ Public subnets for internet-facing resources
✅ Private subnets for backend services
✅ Internet Gateway for public internet access
✅ NAT Gateways for secure outbound connectivity

title: 2.2 Create Security Groups
content:
Security groups act as virtual firewalls that control inbound and outbound traffic for AWS resources. We’ll create specific security groups for each component of our caching architecture.
Security Group Architecture We’ll create four security groups:
Application Security Group (app-sg) - For EC2 instances Redis Security Group (redis-sg) - For ElastiCache DAX Security Group (dax-sg) - For DynamoDB DAX Load Balancer Security Group (alb-sg) - For Application Load Balancer Step 1: Navigate to Security Groups In the VPC Console, click Security Groups in the left navigation
Click Create security group
Step 2: Create Application Security Group Basic Configuration Configure the application security group:
Security group name: app-sg Description: Security group for application servers VPC: Select your caching-workshop-vpc Inbound Rules Add inbound rules for the application: Rule 1: HTTP Access
Type: HTTP Protocol: TCP Port range: 80 Source: 0.0.0.0/0 Description: HTTP access from internet Rule 2: Application Port
Type: Custom TCP Protocol: TCP Port range: 3000 Source: 0.0.0.0/0 Description: Application port access Rule 3: SSH Access
Type: SSH Protocol: TCP Port range: 22 Source: My IP Description: SSH access for management Outbound Rules Keep the default outbound rule (All traffic to 0.0.0.0/0) Click Create security group Step 3: Create Redis Security Group Basic Configuration Create the Redis security group:
Security group name: redis-sg Description: Security group for ElastiCache Redis VPC: Select your caching-workshop-vpc Inbound Rules Add inbound rule for Redis: Rule 1: Redis Access
Type: Custom TCP Protocol: TCP Port range: 6379 Source: Custom (select app-sg) Description: Redis access from application servers We’re allowing access only from the application security group, following the principle of least privilege.
Click Create security group Step 4: Create DAX Security Group Basic Configuration Create the DAX security group:
Security group name: dax-sg Description: Security group for DynamoDB DAX VPC: Select your caching-workshop-vpc Inbound Rules Add inbound rule for DAX: Rule 1: DAX Access
Type: Custom TCP Protocol: TCP Port range: 8111 Source: Custom (select app-sg) Description: DAX access from application servers Click Create security group Step 5: Create Load Balancer Security Group Basic Configuration Create the load balancer security group:
Security group name: alb-sg Description: Security group for Application Load Balancer VPC: Select your caching-workshop-vpc Inbound Rules Add inbound rules for the load balancer: Rule 1: HTTP Access
Type: HTTP Protocol: TCP Port range: 80 Source: 0.0.0.0/0 Description: HTTP access from internet Rule 2: HTTPS Access (Optional)
Type: HTTPS Protocol: TCP Port range: 443 Source: 0.0.0.0/0 Description: HTTPS access from internet Click Create security group Step 6: Verify Security Group Configuration Security Groups Overview View all created security groups: Step 7: Document Security Group IDs Record the security group IDs for use in subsequent steps:
Security Group Information Application SG: sg-xxxxxxxxx (app-sg) Redis SG: sg-xxxxxxxxx (redis-sg) DAX SG: sg-xxxxxxxxx (dax-sg) Load Balancer SG: sg-xxxxxxxxx (alb-sg) Security Best Practices Implemented ✅ Principle of Least Privilege: Each security group only allows necessary traffic
✅ Defense in Depth: Multiple layers of security controls
✅ Source-Based Access: Using security groups as sources instead of IP ranges
✅ Port Specificity: Only opening required ports
✅ Management Access: SSH access restricted to your IP
Troubleshooting Common Issues Issue: Cannot Select Security Group as Source Cause: Security groups must be in the same VPC
Solution: Verify all security groups are created in the correct VPC
Issue: Application Cannot Connect to Redis/DAX Cause: Security group rules not properly configured
Solution:
Verify port numbers (Redis: 6379, DAX: 8111) Confirm source security group is correct Check outbound rules allow traffic Issue: Internet Access Not Working Cause: Security group blocking traffic or routing issues
Solution:
Verify inbound rules allow HTTP/HTTPS Check route tables point to Internet Gateway Confirm NAT Gateway configuration for private subnets Next Steps Your network security is now properly configured! You have:
✅ Application Security Group for EC2 instances
✅ Redis Security Group for ElastiCache access
✅ DAX Security Group for DynamoDB DAX access
✅ Load Balancer Security Group for internet traffic
✅ Least-privilege access between components
✅ Proper traffic flow from internet to backend services
Security groups are stateful, meaning if you allow inbound traffic on a port, the corresponding outbound traffic is automatically allowed.
Next, we’ll set up DynamoDB and DAX for our database layer with caching.

title: 3. Setup DynamoDB and DAX
content:
Setup DynamoDB and DAX In this section, we’ll set up our database layer with DynamoDB as the primary data store and DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) as the database-level cache.
DynamoDB Overview Amazon DynamoDB provides:
Fully managed NoSQL database with single-digit millisecond performance Automatic scaling based on traffic patterns Built-in security with encryption at rest and in transit Global tables for multi-region replication DAX Overview DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) delivers:
Microsecond latency for cached reads (up to 10x faster) Write-through caching maintaining data consistency Automatic cache management with configurable TTL Multi-AZ deployment for high availability Architecture Benefits Our DynamoDB + DAX setup provides:
L2 Cache Layer: DAX serves as the second caching layer after Redis Seamless Integration: DAX is API-compatible with DynamoDB Automatic Failover: Graceful degradation from DAX to DynamoDB Cost Optimization: Reduced DynamoDB read capacity consumption Data Model We’ll create a product catalog with:
Partition Key: ProductID (e.g., PROD001, PROD002) Sort Key: Category (e.g., Electronics, Books) Attributes: Name, Price, Description, Stock, etc. Performance Expectations With DynamoDB + DAX:
DynamoDB Direct: ~10-20ms response time DAX Cache Hit: ~1-2ms response time (microsecond latency) Cache Hit Ratio: 80%+ for frequently accessed items Throughput: 1M+ requests per second with DAX Setup Steps Create DynamoDB Table - Set up the primary data store with sample data Setup DAX Cluster - Configure the database-level cache for microsecond performance DAX is transparent to your application - you can use the same DynamoDB SDK calls, and DAX will automatically cache the results for faster subsequent access.

title: 3.2 Setup DynamoDB DAX
content:
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a fully managed, highly available, in-memory cache for DynamoDB that delivers up to 10x performance improvement. In this step, we’ll create a DAX cluster to provide microsecond-latency access to our ProductCatalog table.
DAX Architecture Overview DAX provides:
Microsecond latency for cached reads Write-through caching for consistency Automatic cache management with TTL Multi-AZ deployment for high availability Step 1: Create DAX Subnet Group Navigate to DAX Console In the DynamoDB Console, click DAX in the left navigation
Click Subnet groups in the left menu
Click Create subnet group Configure Subnet Group Enter subnet group details:
Subnet group name: dax-subnet-group Description: Subnet group for DAX cluster VPC ID: Select your caching-workshop-vpc Select availability zones and subnets: Choose both private subnets from different AZs This ensures high availability for the DAX cluster Click Create subnet group Step 2: Create IAM Role for DAX Navigate to IAM Console Open the IAM Console in a new tab Click Roles → Create role Configure Role Select trusted entity: Trusted entity type: AWS service Service: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) Click Next Attach Permissions Search for and select the following policies: AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess (for workshop purposes) In production, use more restrictive policies following the principle of least privilege. Create custom policies that only allow access to specific DynamoDB tables.
Click Next Name and Create Role Configure role details: Role name: DAXServiceRole Description: Service role for DynamoDB DAX cluster Click Create role Step 3: Create DAX Parameter Group (Optional) Navigate to Parameter Groups Return to the DAX Console Click Parameter groups in the left menu Click Create parameter group Configure Parameter Group Enter parameter group details: Parameter group name: dax-custom-params Description: Custom parameters for DAX cluster Click Create For this workshop, we’ll use default parameters. In production, you might want to tune parameters like query-ttl-millis and record-ttl-millis.
Step 4: Create DAX Cluster Start Cluster Creation Click Clusters in the left navigation Click Create cluster Step 1: Choose Cluster Nodes Enter cluster configuration:
Cluster name: product-dax-cluster Description: DAX cluster for product catalog caching Node type: dax.t3.small Cluster size: 3 nodes 3 nodes provide high availability across multiple AZs. For production workloads, consider larger node types based on your memory and throughput requirements.
Click Next Step 2: Configure Networks Configure VPC settings:
VPC ID: Select vpc-xxxxxxxxx (caching-workshop-vpc) The VPC environment where your DAX cluster will run Configure subnets:
Subnets: Click Choose subnets Select both private subnets from different AZs DAX will select IP addresses from those subnets and assign them to cluster nodes Configure access control:
Security Group: Select dax-sg (replace default security group) A security group acts as a firewall that controls network access to your DAX cluster Click Next Step 3: Configure Security Configure IAM service role:

title: 4. Setup ElastiCache Redis
content:

Step 1: Navigate to ElastiCache Console Open the AWS Management Console Navigate to the ElastiCache service Click Get started or Create if this is your first time Step 2: Create Subnet Group Navigate to Subnet Groups Click Subnet groups in the left navigation
Click Create subnet group
Configure Subnet Group Enter subnet group details:
Name: redis-subnet-group Description: Subnet group for Redis cluster VPC ID: Select your caching-workshop-vpc Select availability zones and subnets:

Choose Deployment Option Select deployment option: Deployment option: Design your own cache This allows us to select specific node types and configurations Serverless option automatically scales but “Design your own cache” gives us more control over node types and costs for this workshop.
Choose Creation Method Select creation method: Creation method: New cache Restore from backup: Not selected (we’re creating a new empty cache) Configure Cache Settings Configure basic cache information:
Name: product-cache Description: Redis cache for product catalog caching Configure Default Settings Configure cache specifications: Use default settings: Uncheck to customize Engine version: 7.2 (latest stable) Port: 6379 Node type: cache.t3.micro Multi-AZ: Enabled Replicas: 1 Multi-AZ with replicas provides high availability and automatic failover capabilities.

Maintenance window: No preference Topic for SNS notification: None (for workshop) Log Settings Configure logging (optional):
Log format: Text Log destination: None (for workshop) Step 6: Review and Create Review Configuration Review all settings
Verify:
Cache name and description Engine version and node type Network and security configuration Backup and maintenance settings Click Create Redis OSS cache

Step 7: Monitor Cache Creation Check Creation Progress Monitor the cache creation progress

Step 8: Note Cache Endpoints Primary Endpoint Note the Primary endpoint for write operations: product-cache.xxxxxx.cache.amazonaws.com:6379 Reader Endpoint Note the Reader endpoint for read operations: product-cache-ro.xxxxxx.cache.amazonaws.com:6379 Step 9: Test Redis Connectivity Launch Test Instance Use the same test EC2 instance from the DAX testing, or launch a new one:
AMI: Amazon Linux 2023 Instance type: t3.micro Subnet: One of your private subnets Security group: app-sg Install Redis CLI Connect to your test instance and install Redis CLI: # Update system sudo yum update -y # Install Redis CLI sudo yum install -y redis6 Test Redis Connection Connect to your Redis cache: # Connect to primary endpoint redis-cli -h product-cache.xxxxxx.cache.amazonaws.com -p 6379 Test basic Redis operations: # Test connection PING # Set a test key SET test:key "Hello Redis from Workshop" # Get the key GET test:key # Set with expiration SETEX product:PROD001 300 '{"name":"Laptop Pro","price":999.99}' # Check TTL TTL product:PROD001 # Get product data GET product:PROD001 # Check Redis info INFO server Step 10: Configure Redis for Application Use Set Memory Policy Configure memory eviction policy: # Connect to primary endpoint redis-cli -h product-cache.xxxxxx.cache.amazonaws.com -p 6379 # Set LRU eviction policy CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru # Verify configuration CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy Test Cache Functionality Test cache behavior with TTL: # Set multiple products with different TTLs SETEX product:PROD001 300 '{"id":"PROD001","name":"Laptop Pro","price":999.99,"category":"Electronics"}' SETEX product:PROD002 600 '{"id":"PROD002","name":"Smartphone X","price":699.99,"category":"Electronics"}' SETEX product:PROD003 900 '{"id":"PROD003","name":"Cloud Guide","price":49.99,"category":"Books"}' # Check all keys KEYS product:* # Check TTL for each key TTL product:PROD001 TTL product:PROD002 TTL product:PROD003 # Get cached data GET product:PROD001 Step 11: Monitor Redis Performance Enable CloudWatch Metrics In the ElastiCache console, go to the Monitoring tab

Next, we’ll deploy our Node.js application that will utilize both Redis and DAX for multi-layer caching.

title: 5. Setup Application
content:
Setup Application In this section, we’ll deploy our Node.js application that demonstrates multi-layer caching architecture. The application will integrate with all the caching layers we’ve set up.
Application Architecture Our caching application includes:
Node.js REST API with Express framework Multi-layer cache integration (Redis → DAX → DynamoDB) Health check endpoints for monitoring Cache statistics and performance metrics Automatic cache warming capabilities Cache Flow The application implements intelligent cache layering:
L1 Cache (Redis): Application-level caching with sub-millisecond access L2 Cache (DAX): Database-level caching with microsecond latency L3 Storage (DynamoDB): Primary data store with consistent performance API Endpoints The application provides these key endpoints:
GET /health - Health check endpoint GET /product/:id - Get product by ID with caching GET /products - List all products with caching GET /stats - Cache performance statistics POST /cache/warmup - Warm up cache with popular items DELETE /cache - Clear Redis cache Performance Benefits With multi-layer caching enabled:
90%+ faster response times compared to direct database access 70%+ reduction in database load through intelligent caching High availability with automatic failover between cache layers Scalable architecture supporting 1000+ concurrent users Setup Steps Launch EC2 Instance - Create and configure the application server Deploy Application - Install and configure the Node.js application The application is designed to gracefully degrade through cache layers, ensuring high availability even if individual cache layers are unavailable.

Size: 8 GiB (default) Volume type: gp3 IOPS: 3000 Throughput: 125 MB/s Step 5: Add User Data Script Advanced Details Expand Advanced details section User Data Script Add the following user data script to automatically install Node.js and dependencies: #!/bin/bash # Update system yum update -y # Install development tools yum groupinstall -y "Development Tools" yum install -y git # Install Node.js using NodeSource repository curl -fsSL https://rpm.nodesource.com/setup_18.x | bash - yum install -y nodejs # Install PM2 for process management npm install -g pm2 # Create application directory mkdir -p /home/ec2-user/caching-app chown ec2-user:ec2-user /home/ec2-user/caching-app # Install CloudWatch agent yum install -y amazon-cloudwatch-agent # Create log directory mkdir -p /var/log/caching-app chown ec2-user:ec2-user /var/log/caching-app # Set up environment echo 'export NODE_ENV=production' >> /home/ec2-user/.bashrc echo 'export PATH=$PATH:/usr/bin' >> /home/ec2-user/.bashrc # Log completion echo "User data script completed at $(date)" >> /var/log/user-data.log The user data script runs automatically when the instance first boots. title: 5.2 Deploy Application
content:
In this step, we’ll deploy our Node.js application that implements the multi-layer caching strategy. The application will demonstrate how to efficiently use Redis, DAX, and DynamoDB together.
Step 1: Prepare Application Directory Navigate to Application Directory SSH into your EC2 instance and navigate to the application directory: cd /home/ec2-user/caching-app Initialize Node.js Project Initialize the npm project: # Initialize package.json npm init -y # Update package.json name sed -i 's/"name": "caching-app"/"name": "multi-layer-caching-app"/' package.json Step 2: Install Dependencies Install Required Packages Install all required dependencies: # Core dependencies npm install express redis aws-sdk amazon-dax-client # Utility dependencies npm install dotenv cors helmet morgan # Development dependencies npm install --save-dev nodemon Verify Installation Check installed packages: # List installed packages npm list --depth=0 # Check package.json cat package.json Step 3: Create Environment Configuration Create Environment File Create .env file with your configuration: nano .env Add your configuration (replace with your actual endpoints): # Redis Configuration REDIS_ENDPOINT=product-cache.xxxxxx.cache.amazonaws.com REDIS_PORT=6379 # DAX Configuration DAX_ENDPOINT=product-dax-cluster.xxxxxx.dax-clusters.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:8111 # DynamoDB Configuration DYNAMODB_TABLE=ProductCatalog AWS_REGION=us-east-1 # Application Configuration PORT=3000 NODE_ENV=production # Cache TTL (seconds) REDIS_TTL=300 DAX_TTL=600 # Logging LOG_LEVEL=info Replace the endpoint URLs with your actual Redis and DAX cluster endpoints from the previous steps.
Step 4: Create Main Application File Create Application Code Create the main application file: nano app.js Add the complete application code: const express = require('express'); const redis = require('redis'); const AWS = require('aws-sdk'); const AmazonDaxClient = require('amazon-dax-client'); const cors = require('cors'); const helmet = require('helmet'); const morgan = require('morgan'); require('dotenv').config(); const app = express(); const PORT = process.env.PORT || 3000; // Middleware app.use(helmet()); app.use(cors()); app.use(morgan('combined')); app.use(express.json()); // Cache statistics let cacheStats = { redis_hits: 0, dax_hits: 0, dynamodb_hits: 0, total_requests: 0, errors: 0 }; // Redis client setup const redisClient = redis.createClient({ host: process.env.REDIS_ENDPOINT, port: process.env.REDIS_PORT, retry_strategy: (options) => { if (options.error && options.error.code === 'ECONNREFUSED') { console.error('Redis server connection refused'); return new Error('Redis server connection refused'); } if (options.total_retry_time > 1000 * 60 * 60) { console.error('Redis retry time exhausted'); return new Error('Redis retry time exhausted'); } if (options.attempt > 10) { return undefined; } return Math.min(options.attempt * 100, 3000); } }); // Handle Redis connection events redisClient.on('connect', () => { console.log('✅ Connected to Redis'); }); redisClient.on('error', (err) => { console.error('❌ Redis connection error:', err.message); }); // AWS Configuration AWS.config.update({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION }); // DynamoDB client setup const dynamodb = new AWS.DynamoDB.DocumentClient(); // DAX client setup let daxClient; try { daxClient = new AmazonDaxClient({ endpoints: [process.env.DAX_ENDPOINT], region: process.env.AWS_REGION }); console.log('✅ DAX client initialized'); } catch (error) { console.error('❌ DAX client initialization failed:', error.message); daxClient = dynamodb; // Fallback to regular DynamoDB } // Health check endpoint app.get('/health', (req, res) => { res.json({ status: 'healthy', timestamp: new Date().toISOString(), uptime: process.uptime(), memory: process.memoryUsage(), version: '1.0.0' }); }); // Get cache statistics app.get('/stats', (req, res) => { const totalCacheHits = cacheStats.redis_hits + cacheStats.dax_hits; const hitRate = cacheStats.total_requests > 0 ? ((totalCacheHits / cacheStats.total_requests) * 100).toFixed(2) : 0; res.json({ ...cacheStats, cache_hit_rate: `${hitRate}%`, redis_hit_rate: cacheStats.total_requests > 0 ? ((cacheStats.redis_hits / cacheStats.total_requests) * 100).toFixed(2) + '%' : '0%', dax_hit_rate: cacheStats.total_requests > 0 ? ((cacheStats.dax_hits / cacheStats.total_requests) * 100).toFixed(2) + '%' : '0%', timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }); }); // Get product with multi-layer caching app.get('/product/:id', async (req, res) => { const productId = req.params.id; const category = req.query.category || 'Electronics'; const cacheKey = `product:${productId}:${category}`; const startTime = Date.now(); cacheStats.total_requests++; try { // Layer 1: Check Redis cache try { const cachedProduct = await redisClient.get(cacheKey); if (cachedProduct) { cacheStats.redis_hits++; const responseTime = Date.now() - startTime; console.log(`🚀 Cache HIT - Redis (${responseTime}ms) - ${cacheKey}`); return res.json({ data: JSON.parse(cachedProduct), source: 'redis-cache', response_time_ms: responseTime, cache_key: cacheKey, timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }); } } catch (redisError) { console.warn('⚠️ Redis error:', redisError.message); cacheStats.errors++; } // Layer 2: Check DAX cache const params = { TableName: process.env.DYNAMODB_TABLE, Key: { ProductID: productId, Category: category } }; try { const daxResult = await daxClient.get(params).promise(); if (daxResult.Item) { cacheStats.dax_hits++; const responseTime = Date.now() - startTime; console.log(`⚡ Cache HIT - DAX (${responseTime}ms) - ${productId}`); // Store in Redis for next time try { await redisClient.setex(cacheKey, process.env.REDIS_TTL, JSON.stringify(daxResult.Item)); console.log(`📝 Cached in Redis: ${cacheKey}`); } catch (redisError) { console.warn('⚠️ Redis set error:', redisError.message); } return res.json({ data: daxResult.Item, source: 'dax-cache', response_time_ms: responseTime, cache_key: cacheKey, timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }); } } catch (daxError) { console.warn('⚠️ DAX error:', daxError.message); cacheStats.errors++; } // Layer 3: Fallback to DynamoDB try { const dynamoResult = await dynamodb.get(params).promise(); if (dynamoResult.Item) { cacheStats.dynamodb_hits++; const responseTime = Date.now() - startTime; console.log(`🐌 Cache MISS - DynamoDB (${responseTime}ms) - ${productId}`); // Store in Redis for future requests try { await redisClient.setex(cacheKey, process.env.REDIS_TTL, JSON.stringify(dynamoResult.Item)); console.log(`📝 Cached in Redis: ${cacheKey}`); } catch (redisError) { console.warn('⚠️ Redis set error:', redisError.message); } return res.json({ data: dynamoResult.Item, source: 'dynamodb', response_time_ms: responseTime, cache_key: cacheKey, timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }); } } catch (dynamoError) { console.error('❌ DynamoDB error:', dynamoError.message); cacheStats.errors++; } // Product not found res.status(404).json({ error: 'Product not found', product_id: productId, category: category, timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }); } catch (error) { console.error('❌ Unexpected error:', error); cacheStats.errors++; res.status(500).json({ error: 'Internal server error', message: error.message, timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }); } }); // Get all products (with caching) app.get('/products', async (req, res) => { const category = req.query.category; const cacheKey = category ? `products:category:${category}` : 'products:all'; const startTime = Date.now(); cacheStats.total_requests++; try { // Check Redis first try { const cachedProducts = await redisClient.get(cacheKey); if (cachedProducts) { cacheStats.redis_hits++; const responseTime = Date.now() - startTime; console.log(`🚀 Products Cache HIT - Redis (${responseTime}ms)`); return res.json({ data: JSON.parse(cachedProducts), source: 'redis-cache', response_time_ms: responseTime, cache_key: cacheKey, timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }); } } catch (redisError) { console.warn('⚠️ Redis error:', redisError.message); } // Query DynamoDB let params = { TableName: process.env.DYNAMODB_TABLE }; if (category) { params = { ...params, FilterExpression: 'Category = :category', ExpressionAttributeValues: { ':category': category } }; } const result = await dynamodb.scan(params).promise(); const responseTime = Date.now() - startTime; cacheStats.dynamodb_hits++; console.log(`🐌 Products Cache MISS - DynamoDB (${responseTime}ms)`); // Cache the results with shorter TTL for lists try { await redisClient.setex(cacheKey, 60, JSON.stringify(result.Items)); console.log(`📝 Cached products in Redis: ${cacheKey}`); } catch (redisError) { console.warn('⚠️ Redis set error:', redisError.message); } res.json({ data: result.Items, count: result.Items.length, source: 'dynamodb', response_time_ms: responseTime, cache_key: cacheKey, timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }); } catch (error) { console.error('❌ Error fetching products:', error); cacheStats.errors++; res.status(500).json({ error: 'Internal server error', message: error.message, timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }); } }); // Clear specific cache app.delete('/cache/:key', async (req, res) => { try { const key = req.params.key; const cacheKey = key.startsWith('product:') ? key : `product:${key}`; const result = await redisClient.del(cacheKey); console.log(`🗑️ Cache cleared: ${cacheKey}`); res.json({ message: 'Cache cleared', cache_key: cacheKey, keys_deleted: result, timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }); } catch (error) { console.error('❌ Cache clear error:', error); res.status(500).json({ error: 'Failed to clear cache', message: error.message, timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }); } }); // Clear all cache app.delete('/cache', async (req, res) => { try { await redisClient.flushall(); console.log('🗑️ All cache cleared'); res.json({ message: 'All cache cleared', timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }); } catch (error) { console.error('❌ Cache flush error:', error); res.status(500).json({ error: 'Failed to clear cache', message: error.message, timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }); } }); // Warm up cache endpoint app.post('/cache/warmup', async (req, res) => { try { console.log('🔥 Starting cache warmup...'); const params = { TableName: process.env.DYNAMODB_TABLE }; const result = await dynamodb.scan(params).promise(); let warmedUp = 0; for (const item of result.Items) { const cacheKey = `product:${item.ProductID}:${item.Category}`; try { await redisClient.setex(cacheKey, process.env.REDIS_TTL, JSON.stringify(item)); warmedUp++; console.log(`🔥 Warmed up: ${cacheKey}`); } catch (redisError) { console.warn(`⚠️ Failed to warm up ${cacheKey}:`, redisError.message); } } console.log(`🔥 Cache warmup completed: ${warmedUp}/${result.Items.length} items`); res.json({ message: 'Cache warmed up successfully', products_cached: warmedUp, total_products: result.Items.length, timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }); } catch (error) { console.error('❌ Cache warmup error:', error); res.status(500).json({ error: 'Cache warmup failed', message: error.message, timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }); } }); // Reset statistics app.post('/stats/reset', (req, res) => { cacheStats = { redis_hits: 0, dax_hits: 0, dynamodb_hits: 0, total_requests: 0, errors: 0 }; console.log('📊 Statistics reset'); res.json({ message: 'Statistics reset successfully', timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }); }); // Start server app.listen(PORT, '0.0.0.0', () => { console.log(`🚀 Multi-layer caching application started`); console.log(`🌐 Server running on port ${PORT}`); console.log(`📊 Health check: http://localhost:${PORT}/health`); console.log(`📈 Statistics: http://localhost:${PORT}/stats`); console.log(`🔥 Cache warmup: POST http://localhost:${PORT}/cache/warmup`); }); // Graceful shutdown process.on('SIGTERM', () => { console.log('🛑 SIGTERM received, shutting down gracefully'); redisClient.quit(); process.exit(0); }); process.on('SIGINT', () => { console.log('🛑 SIGINT received, shutting down gracefully'); redisClient.quit(); process.exit(0); }); Step 5: Update Package.json Scripts Add NPM Scripts Update package.json to add useful scripts: nano package.json Add these scripts to the scripts section: { "name": "multi-layer-caching-app", "version": "1.0.0", "description": "Multi-layer caching application with Redis, DAX, and DynamoDB", "main": "app.js", "scripts": { "start": "node app.js", "dev": "nodemon app.js", "pm2:start": "pm2 start app.js --name caching-app --log /var/log/caching-app/app.log", "pm2:stop": "pm2 stop caching-app", "pm2:restart": "pm2 restart caching-app", "pm2:logs": "pm2 logs caching-app", "pm2:status": "pm2 status", "test": "echo \"Error: no test specified\" && exit 1" }, "keywords": ["caching", "redis", "dax", "dynamodb", "aws", "performance"], "author": "Workshop Participant", "license": "MIT" } Step 6: Test Application Locally Start Application Test the application locally first: # Start the application npm start Test Health Endpoint In another terminal, test the health endpoint: # Test health check curl http://your-instance-public-ip:3000/health Test Product Endpoint Test product retrieval: # Test product endpoint curl "http://your-instance-public-ip:3000/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" Test Cache Statistics Check cache statistics: # Check stats curl http://your-instance-public-ip:3000/stats Step 7: Deploy with PM2 Stop Development Server Stop the development server (Ctrl+C) and start with PM2: # Start with PM2 npm run pm2:start Check PM2 Status Verify PM2 is running the application: # Check PM2 status npm run pm2:status View Application Logs Monitor application logs: # View logs npm run pm2:logs Step 8: Performance Testing Test Cache Performance Test the caching behavior by making multiple requests: # First request (cache miss) time curl "http://your-instance-public-ip:3000/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" # Second request (cache hit) time curl "http://your-instance-public-ip:3000/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" # Check statistics curl http://your-instance-public-ip:3000/stats Load Testing Perform basic load testing: # Install Apache Bench (if not available) sudo yum install -y httpd-tools # Run load test ab -n 100 -c 10 http://your-instance-public-ip:3000/product/PROD001?category=Electronics Step 9: Configure Application Monitoring PM2 Monitoring Enable PM2 monitoring: # Enable PM2 monitoring pm2 install pm2-logrotate # Set log rotation pm2 set pm2-logrotate:max_size 10M pm2 set pm2-logrotate:retain 7 Application Logs Check application logs location: # View log files ls -la /var/log/caching-app/ # Tail application logs tail -f /var/log/caching-app/app.log Step 11: Document Application Configuration Record the following information:
Application Information Application Name: multi-layer-caching-app Port: 3000 Process Manager: PM2 Log Location: /var/log/caching-app/app.log API Endpoints Health Check: GET /health Get Product: GET /product/:id?category=:category Get Products: GET /products?category=:category Cache Stats: GET /stats Clear Cache: DELETE /cache/:key Warm Cache: POST /cache/warmup Reset Stats: POST /stats/reset Performance Characteristics Cold Start: ~500ms (DynamoDB) Warm Cache (DAX): ~10ms Hot Cache (Redis): ~1ms Expected Hit Rate: 90%+ Troubleshooting Common Issues Issue: Application Won’t Start Possible Causes:
Missing dependencies Environment configuration errors Port conflicts Solutions:
Run npm install to ensure all dependencies are installed Check .env file for correct endpoint URLs Verify port 3000 is not in use: netstat -tlnp | grep 3000 Issue: Cannot Connect to Redis/DAX Possible Causes:
Incorrect endpoint URLs Security group restrictions Network connectivity issues Solutions:
Verify endpoint URLs in .env file Check security groups allow traffic on ports 6379 (Redis) and 8111 (DAX) Test connectivity: telnet redis-endpoint 6379 Issue: High Error Rate Possible Causes:
Service unavailability IAM permission issues Network timeouts Solutions:
Check CloudWatch logs for specific errors Verify IAM role has necessary permissions Monitor service health in AWS console Next Steps Your multi-layer caching application is now deployed and running! You have:
✅ Node.js Application with Express framework
✅ Multi-layer Caching implementation
✅ Redis Integration for L1 caching
✅ DAX Integration for L2 caching
✅ DynamoDB Fallback as source of truth
✅ PM2 Process Management for production
✅ Comprehensive API for testing and monitoring
✅ Performance Monitoring with statistics
Application Features: Intelligent Cache Fallback: Redis → DAX → DynamoDB Performance Tracking: Response times and hit rates Cache Management: Warmup, clearing, and statistics Error Handling: Graceful degradation when services are unavailable Production Ready: PM2 process management and logging Monitor the application logs with pm2 logs caching-app to see the caching behavior in real-time and understand the performance improvements.
Next, we’ll set up an Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic and provide high availability for our application.

title: 6. Setup Application Load Balancer
content:
In this step, we’ll create an Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic to our caching application and provide high availability.
Step 1: Create Target Group Navigate to Target Groups Open the EC2 Console
Click Target Groups in the left navigation
Click Create target group
Configure Target Group Configure basic settings:
Target type: Instances Target group name: caching-app-tg Protocol: HTTP Port: 3000 VPC: Select your caching-workshop-vpc Configure Health Checks Configure health check settings:
Health check protocol: HTTP Health check path: /health Health check port: Traffic port Healthy threshold: 2 Unhealthy threshold: 2 Timeout: 5 seconds Interval: 30 seconds Click Next Register Targets Select your application instance:
Find your caching-app-server instance Select it and click Include as pending below Click Create target group Step 2: Verify Target Health Check Target Health Click on your target group to view details Go to the Targets tab and verify health status It may take 1-2 minutes for the target to become healthy. The health check calls /health endpoint on port 3000.
Step 3: Create Application Load Balancer Navigate to Load Balancers Click Load Balancers in the left navigation Click Create load balancer Choose Load Balancer Type Select Application Load Balancer Click Create Configure Basic Settings Configure load balancer settings:
Load balancer name: caching-app-alb Scheme: Internet-facing IP address type: IPv4 Configure Network Mapping Configure network settings:
VPC: Select your caching-workshop-vpc Mappings: Select both public subnets from different AZs Configure Security Groups Configure security groups:
Security groups: Select alb-sg Remove the default security group Configure Listeners Configure listeners and routing:
Protocol: HTTP Port: 80 Default action: Forward to caching-app-tg Step 4: Review and Create Review Configuration Review all settings Click Create load balancer Load balancer creation takes 2-3 minutes. The load balancer will show “Provisioning” status initially.
Step 5: Verify Load Balancer Check Load Balancer Status Wait for the load balancer to become “Active” Note the DNS name for testing: caching-app-alb-xxxxxxxxx.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com Step 6: Test Load Balancer Test Health Endpoint Test the load balancer using its DNS name: # Test health endpoint through ALB curl http://caching-app-alb-xxxxxxxxx.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com/health Test Application Endpoints Test all application endpoints through the load balancer: # Test product endpoint curl "http://caching-app-alb-xxxxxxxxx.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" # Test products list curl "http://caching-app-alb-xxxxxxxxx.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com/products" # Test cache statistics curl http://caching-app-alb-xxxxxxxxx.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com/stats Step 7: Configure Additional Features Enable Access Logs (Optional) Go to the Attributes tab of your load balancer Click Edit and enable access logs:
Access logs: Enabled S3 location: Create or select S3 bucket Configure Sticky Sessions (Optional) In your target group, go to Attributes tab:
Stickiness: Enabled Stickiness type: Load balancer generated cookie Stickiness duration: 1 day Step 8: Monitor Load Balancer CloudWatch Metrics Go to the Monitoring tab to view metrics Key metrics to monitor:
RequestCount: Number of requests TargetResponseTime: Response time from targets HTTPCode_Target_2XX_Count: Successful responses HTTPCode_Target_4XX_Count: Client errors HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count: Server errors Set Up CloudWatch Alarms Create alarms for key metrics: # High response time alarm aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \ --alarm-name "ALB-High-Response-Time" \ --alarm-description "ALB response time is high" \ --metric-name TargetResponseTime \ --namespace AWS/ApplicationELB \ --statistic Average \ --period 300 \ --threshold 1.0 \ --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \ --evaluation-periods 2 Step 9: Test High Availability Simulate Instance Failure Stop your EC2 instance to test failover: # Stop the instance (simulate failure) aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Check target group health Test load balancer response: # This should return 503 Service Unavailable curl http://caching-app-alb-xxxxxxxxx.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com/health Restore Service Start the instance again: # Start the instance aws ec2 start-instances --instance-ids i-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Wait for target to become healthy again Step 10: Document Load Balancer Configuration Record the following information:
Load Balancer Information Load Balancer Name: caching-app-alb DNS Name: caching-app-alb-xxxxxxxxx.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com Scheme: Internet-facing Security Group: alb-sg Target Group: caching-app-tg Configuration Details Listener: HTTP:80 → Forward to target group Health Check: HTTP:3000/health Health Check Interval: 30 seconds Healthy Threshold: 2 consecutive checks Troubleshooting Common Issues Issue: Targets Showing Unhealthy Possible Causes:
Application not responding on health check path Security group blocking traffic Instance not running Solutions:
Verify application is running: pm2 status Check health endpoint directly: curl localhost:3000/health Verify security groups allow traffic on port 3000 Issue: 502 Bad Gateway Errors Possible Causes:
Application crashed or not responding Target group pointing to wrong port Network connectivity issues Solutions:
Check application logs: pm2 logs caching-app Verify target group port configuration Test direct instance connectivity Issue: Load Balancer Not Accessible Possible Causes:
Security group not allowing HTTP traffic Load balancer in wrong subnets DNS propagation delay Solutions:
Verify ALB security group allows HTTP (port 80) Ensure load balancer is in public subnets Wait for DNS propagation (up to 5 minutes) Performance Optimization Connection Draining Deregistration delay: 300 seconds (default) Allows in-flight requests to complete before removing targets Health Check Tuning Faster detection: Reduce interval and threshold for quicker failover Reduce false positives: Increase threshold for stable applications Multiple Targets Auto Scaling: Add multiple instances for higher availability Cross-AZ: Distribute targets across availability zones Next Steps Your Application Load Balancer is now configured and tested! You have:
✅ Application Load Balancer distributing traffic
✅ Target Group with health checks configured
✅ High availability across multiple AZs
✅ Health monitoring with automatic failover
✅ CloudWatch metrics for performance monitoring
✅ Security groups properly configured
Load Balancer Benefits: High availability: Automatic failover when instances fail Scalability: Easy to add more instances behind the load balancer Health monitoring: Continuous health checks ensure traffic goes to healthy instances SSL termination: Can handle SSL/TLS encryption (when configured) The load balancer DNS name will be used by CloudFront in the next step as the origin for our CDN distribution.
Next, we’ll set up CloudFront to provide global content delivery and edge caching.

title: 7. Setup CloudFront CDN
content:
In this step, we’ll create a CloudFront distribution to provide global edge caching for our multi-layer caching application.
Step 1: Navigate to CloudFront Console Open the AWS Management Console Navigate to the CloudFront service Click Create distribution Step 2: Configure Origin Settings Origin Domain Configure the origin settings:
Origin domain: Enter your ALB DNS name caching-app-alb-xxxxxxxxx.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com Protocol: HTTP only (for workshop) HTTP port: 80 Origin Path Configure origin path (optional):
Origin path: Leave empty Name: Auto-generated based on domain Additional Origin Settings Configure additional settings:
Add custom header: None Enable Origin Shield: No (for workshop) Step 3: Configure Default Cache Behavior Path Pattern Configure cache behavior:
Path pattern: Default (*) Compress objects automatically: Yes Viewer Protocol Policy Configure viewer protocol:
Viewer protocol policy: Redirect HTTP to HTTPS Allowed HTTP methods: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, POST, PATCH, DELETE Cache Key and Origin Requests Configure cache key settings:
Cache policy: Create new policy or use existing Origin request policy: None Response headers policy: None Create Custom Cache Policy Click Create policy to create a custom cache policy:
Name: CachingAppPolicy Description: Cache policy for caching application Default TTL: 300 seconds (5 minutes) Maximum TTL: 3600 seconds (1 hour) Minimum TTL: 0 seconds Cache Key Settings Configure cache key settings:
Headers: None Query strings: All Cookies: None Click Create
Step 4: Configure Distribution Settings Price Class Configure distribution settings:
Price class: Use all edge locations (best performance) AWS WAF web ACL: None Alternate Domain Names Configure domain settings:
Alternate domain names (CNAMEs): Leave empty for workshop Custom SSL certificate: Default CloudFront certificate Default Root Object Configure default root object:
Default root object: Leave empty Standard logging: Off (for workshop) Description and Comments Add description:
Description: CloudFront distribution for multi-layer caching workshop Distribution state: Enabled Step 5: Review and Create Review Configuration Review all settings Click Create distribution CloudFront distribution deployment takes 15-20 minutes. The distribution will show “Deploying” status during this time.
Step 6: Monitor Distribution Deployment Check Deployment Status Monitor the distribution deployment The status will change from “Deploying” to “Enabled” Note Distribution Domain Once deployed, note the Distribution domain name: d1234567890123.cloudfront.net Step 7: Test CloudFront Distribution Test Basic Connectivity Test the CloudFront distribution: # Test health endpoint through CloudFront curl https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/health Test Application Endpoints Test all application endpoints: # Test product endpoint curl "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" # Test products list curl "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/products" # Test cache statistics curl https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/stats Step 8: Configure Cache Behaviors Create API Cache Behavior Go to the Behaviors tab and click Create behavior
Configure API-specific caching:
Path pattern: /product/* Origin: Your ALB origin Cache policy: Create new policy for API API Cache Policy Create API cache policy:
Name: APIResponsePolicy Default TTL: 300 seconds Maximum TTL: 600 seconds Query strings: All Headers: Include Authorization if needed Create Stats Behavior Create behavior for stats endpoint:
Path pattern: /stats Cache policy: Create no-cache policy TTL: 0 seconds (no caching) Step 9: Test Cache Performance Test Cache Miss Clear any existing cache and test: # First request (cache miss) time curl "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" Test Cache Hit Make the same request again: # Second request (cache hit) time curl "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" Check Response Headers Check CloudFront cache headers: # Check cache headers curl -I "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" Look for headers like:
X-Cache: Hit from cloudfront (cache hit) X-Cache: Miss from cloudfront (cache miss) Age: 120 (time since cached) Step 10: Configure Cache Invalidation Create Invalidation Go to the Invalidations tab and click Create invalidation
Configure invalidation paths:
Object paths: /product/*/products/stats Click Create invalidation
Monitor Invalidation Monitor invalidation progress Invalidations take 5-15 minutes to complete across all edge locations.
Step 11: Monitor CloudFront Performance CloudWatch Metrics Go to the Monitoring tab to view metrics Key metrics to monitor:
Requests: Number of requests to CloudFront BytesDownloaded: Data transferred to viewers CacheHitRate: Percentage of requests served from cache OriginLatency: Response time from origin 4xxErrorRate: Client error rate 5xxErrorRate: Server error rate Real-time Logs (Optional) Enable real-time logs for detailed monitoring Step 12: Performance Comparison Test Performance Improvement Compare response times: # Direct ALB access time curl "http://caching-app-alb-xxxxxxxxx.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" # CloudFront access (after cache warm-up) time curl "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" Global Performance Test Test from different locations using online tools: GTmetrix: Test from multiple global locations Pingdom: Global performance monitoring WebPageTest: Detailed performance analysis Step 13: Document CloudFront Configuration Record the following information:
CloudFront Distribution Information Distribution ID: E1234567890123 Domain Name: d1234567890123.cloudfront.net Origin: ALB DNS name Status: Enabled Price Class: All edge locations Cache Behaviors Default: 5-minute TTL, all query strings API Endpoints: 5-minute TTL, optimized for API responses Stats Endpoint: No caching for real-time data Performance Characteristics Global latency: 10-50ms (depending on edge location) Cache hit ratio target: 80%+ Origin offload: 70%+ reduction in origin requests Troubleshooting Common Issues Issue: Distribution Not Accessible Possible Causes:
Distribution still deploying Origin not accessible DNS propagation delay Solutions:
Wait for deployment to complete (15-20 minutes) Test origin directly first Use distribution domain name, not custom domain Issue: High Cache Miss Rate Possible Causes:
Query strings not configured properly Headers affecting cache key TTL too short Solutions:
Review cache policy configuration Check query string and header settings Increase TTL for stable content Issue: Origin Errors Possible Causes:
ALB or application issues Security group blocking CloudFront Origin timeout Solutions:
Check ALB and application health Verify security groups allow CloudFront IPs Increase origin timeout settings Security Best Practices Origin Access Control Restrict origin access: Only allow CloudFront to access ALB Security groups: Update ALB security group to only allow CloudFront SSL/TLS Configuration Viewer protocol: Redirect HTTP to HTTPS Origin protocol: Use HTTPS when possible Security headers: Add security headers via response headers policy Next Steps Your CloudFront distribution is now configured and optimized! You have:
✅ Global CDN with edge locations worldwide
✅ Edge caching reducing origin load
✅ Custom cache behaviors for different content types
✅ Cache invalidation for content updates
✅ Performance monitoring with CloudWatch metrics
✅ SSL/TLS termination for secure connections
CloudFront Benefits Achieved: Global performance: Low latency from edge locations worldwide Origin protection: Reduced load on ALB and application servers DDoS protection: Built-in AWS Shield protection Cost optimization: Reduced data transfer costs from origin CloudFront cache hit rates typically improve over time as more content gets cached at edge locations. Monitor the cache hit rate and adjust TTL settings as needed.

title: 8. Performance Testing
content:
In this step, we’ll perform comprehensive load testing to measure the performance improvements achieved by our multi-layer caching architecture.
Step 1: Install Testing Tools Install Apache Bench SSH into your EC2 instance and install testing tools: # Install Apache Bench sudo yum install -y httpd-tools # Install additional tools sudo yum install -y curl wget jq # Verify installation ab -V Install Artillery (Advanced Testing) Install Artillery for more advanced testing: # Install Artillery globally npm install -g artillery # Verify installation artillery version Step 2: Baseline Performance Testing Test Direct DynamoDB Access Clear all caches and test direct database access: # Clear Redis cache curl -X DELETE https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/cache # Reset statistics curl -X POST https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/stats/reset # Test direct database access (cold start) time curl "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" Measure Response Times Record baseline metrics: # Run multiple tests and calculate average for i in {1..10}; do echo "Test $i:" time curl -s "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" > /dev/null done Step 3: Cache Performance Testing Test Redis Cache Performance Warm up Redis cache and test: # Warm up cache curl -X POST https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/cache/warmup # Test Redis cache hit time curl "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" # Check cache statistics curl https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/stats Test DAX Cache Performance Clear Redis but keep DAX cache: # Clear only Redis cache curl -X DELETE https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/cache/product:PROD001:Electronics # Test DAX cache hit time curl "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" Test CloudFront Cache Performance Test CloudFront edge cache: # Make request to warm CloudFront cache curl "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" # Test CloudFront cache hit (check X-Cache header) curl -I "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" # Measure response time time curl -s "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" > /dev/null Step 4: Load Testing with Apache Bench Single Endpoint Load Test Test single product endpoint under load: # Test with 100 requests, 10 concurrent ab -n 100 -c 10 "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" Multiple Endpoints Load Test Test different endpoints: # Test products list endpoint ab -n 100 -c 10 "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/products" # Test health endpoint ab -n 100 -c 10 "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/health" # Test stats endpoint ab -n 50 -c 5 "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/stats" High Concurrency Test Test with higher concurrency: # Test with 1000 requests, 50 concurrent ab -n 1000 -c 50 "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" Step 5: Advanced Testing with Artillery Create Artillery Configuration Create Artillery test configuration: nano artillery-test.yml Add test configuration: config: target: 'https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net' phases: - duration: 60 arrivalRate: 10 name: "Warm up" - duration: 120 arrivalRate: 50 name: "Load test" - duration: 60 arrivalRate: 100 name: "Stress test" defaults: headers: User-Agent: "Artillery Load Test" scenarios: - name: "Product API Test" weight: 70 flow: - get: url: "/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" - get: url: "/product/PROD002?category=Electronics" - get: url: "/product/PROD003?category=Books" - name: "Products List Test" weight: 20 flow: - get: url: "/products" - get: url: "/products?category=Electronics" - name: "Health Check Test" weight: 10 flow: - get: url: "/health" - get: url: "/stats" Run Artillery Test Execute the Artillery test: # Run the load test artillery run artillery-test.yml Step 6: Performance Comparison Analysis Create Performance Comparison Script Create a script to compare performance across layers: nano performance-test.sh Add comparison script: #!/bin/bash echo "=== Multi-Layer Caching Performance Test ===" echo "Testing URL: https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net" echo # Function to test response time test_response_time() { local url=$1 local description=$2 echo "Testing: $description" # Run 5 tests and calculate average total=0 for i in {1..5}; do time_ms=$(curl -o /dev/null -s -w "%{time_total}" "$url" | awk '{print $1*1000}') total=$(echo "$total + $time_ms" | bc) echo " Test $i: ${time_ms}ms" done average=$(echo "scale=2; $total / 5" | bc) echo " Average: ${average}ms" echo } # Clear all caches echo "Clearing all caches..." curl -s -X DELETE https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/cache > /dev/null curl -s -X POST https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/stats/reset > /dev/null sleep 2 # Test 1: Cold start (DynamoDB only) test_response_time "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" "Cold Start (DynamoDB)" # Test 2: DAX cache hit test_response_time "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" "DAX Cache Hit" # Test 3: Redis cache hit test_response_time "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" "Redis Cache Hit" # Test 4: CloudFront cache hit test_response_time "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" "CloudFront Cache Hit" # Get final statistics echo "=== Final Cache Statistics ===" curl -s https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/stats | jq '.' Run the performance comparison: # Make script executable chmod +x performance-test.sh # Run the test ./performance-test.sh Step 7: Monitor System Performance Check Application Metrics Monitor application performance during testing: # Check PM2 process status pm2 status # Monitor application logs pm2 logs caching-app --lines 50 # Check system resources top htop Check AWS Service Metrics Monitor AWS service performance: # Check ElastiCache metrics aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics \ --namespace AWS/ElastiCache \ --metric-name CPUUtilization \ --dimensions Name=CacheClusterId,Value=product-cache-001 \ --start-time 2024-01-15T10:00:00Z \ --end-time 2024-01-15T11:00:00Z \ --period 300 \ --statistics Average # Check DynamoDB metrics aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics \ --namespace AWS/DynamoDB \ --metric-name ConsumedReadCapacityUnits \ --dimensions Name=TableName,Value=ProductCatalog \ --start-time 2024-01-15T10:00:00Z \ --end-time 2024-01-15T11:00:00Z \ --period 300 \ --statistics Sum Step 8: Cache Hit Ratio Analysis Analyze Cache Effectiveness Test cache hit ratios under different scenarios: # Test with random product IDs for i in {1..100}; do product_id="PROD00$((RANDOM % 5 + 1))" curl -s "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/$product_id?category=Electronics" > /dev/null done # Check final statistics curl https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/stats | jq '{ total_requests, redis_hits, dax_hits, dynamodb_hits, cache_hit_rate, redis_hit_rate, dax_hit_rate }' Optimize Cache Performance Test different cache configurations: # Test with cache warmup curl -X POST https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/cache/warmup # Run load test again ab -n 200 -c 20 "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" # Check improved statistics curl https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/stats Step 9: Stress Testing Test System Limits Gradually increase load to find system limits: # Test with increasing concurrency for concurrency in 10 20 50 100 200; content:

Title: Redis Performance Metrics Period: 5 minutes Add Redis Cache Effectiveness Widget Add cache hit/miss metrics:

DistributionId: Your CloudFront distribution ID Add CloudFront Error Widget Add CloudFront error metrics:
Widget type: Line Metrics: 4xxErrorRate, 5xxErrorRate Title: CloudFront Error Rates Step 6: Add Custom Application Metrics Create Custom Metrics Script SSH into your EC2 instance and create a custom metrics script: nano send-custom-metrics.sh Add the custom metrics script: #!/bin/bash # Get application statistics STATS=$(curl -s http://localhost:3000/stats) # Extract metrics using jq TOTAL_REQUESTS=$(echo $STATS | jq -r '.total_requests // 0') REDIS_HITS=$(echo $STATS | jq -r '.redis_hits // 0') DAX_HITS=$(echo $STATS | jq -r '.dax_hits // 0') DYNAMODB_HITS=$(echo $STATS | jq -r '.dynamodb_hits // 0') ERRORS=$(echo $STATS | jq -r '.errors // 0') # Calculate hit rates if [ $TOTAL_REQUESTS -gt 0 ]; then CACHE_HIT_RATE=$(echo "scale=2; ($REDIS_HITS + $DAX_HITS) * 100 / $TOTAL_REQUESTS" | bc) REDIS_HIT_RATE=$(echo "scale=2; $REDIS_HITS * 100 / $TOTAL_REQUESTS" | bc) else CACHE_HIT_RATE=0 REDIS_HIT_RATE=0 fi # Send metrics to CloudWatch aws cloudwatch put-metric-data \ --namespace "CachingApp/Performance" \ --metric-data \ MetricName=TotalRequests,Value=$TOTAL_REQUESTS,Unit=Count \ MetricName=RedisHits,Value=$REDIS_HITS,Unit=Count \ MetricName=DAXHits,Value=$DAX_HITS,Unit=Count \ MetricName=DynamoDBHits,Value=$DYNAMODB_HITS,Unit=Count \ MetricName=Errors,Value=$ERRORS,Unit=Count \ MetricName=CacheHitRate,Value=$CACHE_HIT_RATE,Unit=Percent \ MetricName=RedisHitRate,Value=$REDIS_HIT_RATE,Unit=Percent echo "Custom metrics sent to CloudWatch" Make the script executable: chmod +x send-custom-metrics.sh Set Up Cron Job Set up a cron job to send metrics every minute: # Edit crontab crontab -e # Add this line to run every minute * * * * * /home/ec2-user/caching-app/send-custom-metrics.sh Add Custom Metrics Widget Add custom metrics to dashboard:
Widget type: Line Metrics: CachingApp/Performance Metric names: CacheHitRate, RedisHitRate Title: Application Cache Performance Step 7: Create CloudWatch Alarms Create High Response Time Alarm Navigate to Alarms in CloudWatch
Click Create alarm
Configure ALB response time alarm:
Metric: AWS/ApplicationELB > TargetResponseTime LoadBalancer: caching-app-alb Statistic: Average Period: 5 minutes Set alarm conditions:
Threshold type: Static Condition: Greater than 500 (milliseconds) Datapoints to alarm: 2 out of 3 Configure alarm actions:
Alarm state trigger: In alarm SNS topic: Create new topic caching-alerts Email: Your email address Name the alarm:
Alarm name: High-Response-Time-ALB Description: ALB response time is above 500ms Create Low Cache Hit Rate Alarm Create alarm for low cache hit rate:
Metric: CachingApp/Performance > CacheHitRate Condition: Less than 80 (percent) Name: Low-Cache-Hit-Rate Create High Error Rate Alarm Create alarm for high error rate:
Metric: AWS/ApplicationELB > HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count Condition: Greater than 10 (count) Name: High-Error-Rate-ALB Create Redis High CPU Alarm Create alarm for Redis high CPU:
Metric: AWS/ElastiCache > CPUUtilization CacheClusterId: product-cache-001 Condition: Greater than 80 (percent) Name: Redis-High-CPU Step 8: Configure Log Insights Set Up Log Groups Navigate to Log groups in CloudWatch
Create log group for application logs:
Log group name: /aws/ec2/caching-app Retention: 7 days Configure CloudWatch Agent Install and configure CloudWatch agent on EC2: # Create CloudWatch agent configuration sudo nano /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json Add agent configuration: { "logs": { "logs_collected": { "files": { "collect_list": [ { "file_path": "/var/log/caching-app/app.log", "log_group_name": "/aws/ec2/caching-app", "log_stream_name": "{instance_id}-app.log" } ] } } }, "metrics": { "namespace": "CWAgent", "metrics_collected": { "cpu": { "measurement": [ "cpu_usage_idle", "cpu_usage_iowait", "cpu_usage_user", "cpu_usage_system" ], "metrics_collection_interval": 60 }, "disk": { "measurement": [ "used_percent" ], "metrics_collection_interval": 60, "resources": [ "*" ] }, "mem": { "measurement": [ "mem_used_percent" ], "metrics_collection_interval": 60 } } } } Start CloudWatch agent: # Start the agent sudo /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl \ -a fetch-config \ -m ec2 \ -c file:/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json \ -s Step 9: Create Log Insights Queries Create Performance Query Navigate to Log Insights in CloudWatch
Create query for performance analysis:
fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /Cache HIT|Cache MISS/ | stats count() by bin(5m) | sort @timestamp desc Create Error Analysis Query Create query for error analysis: fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /ERROR|error/ | stats count() by bin(1h) | sort @timestamp desc Step 10: Finalize Dashboard Arrange Dashboard Widgets Arrange widgets in logical order:
Top row: Overall performance (ALB, CloudFront) Middle row: Cache performance (Redis, DAX) Bottom row: Database and custom metrics Save Dashboard Save the dashboard:
Click Save dashboard Verify all widgets are displaying data Step 11: Test Monitoring Setup Generate Test Traffic Generate traffic to populate metrics: # Run load test to generate metrics ab -n 200 -c 20 "https://d1234567890123.cloudfront.net/product/PROD001?category=Electronics" # Wait for metrics to appear (5-10 minutes) Verify Metrics Check that all metrics are appearing in dashboard: Test Alarms Trigger test alarm by stopping application: # Stop application to trigger alarms pm2 stop caching-app # Wait for alarm to trigger (5-10 minutes) Restart application: # Restart application pm2 start caching-app Step 12: Document Monitoring Setup Monitoring Configuration Summary Record the following information:
